title: African Poetry: 'Once Upon a Time' by Gabriel Okara
summary: The poet, the speaker, the meaning, themes, tone and devices of Okara's poem about a father who has learnt to be false and wants to be genuine again.

p: Gabriel Okara (1921 to 2019) was a Nigerian poet and novelist from the Ijaw people of the Niger Delta. His poems often set traditional African values against the cold, false ways of modern society.

A father is speaking to his young son. He remembers a time ('once upon a time', as in a children's story) when people laughed with their hearts and their eyes. Now, in a modern, Westernised and hypocritical world, people laugh only with their teeth, shake hands without feeling, and their cold eyes search behind your shadow. The father himself has also learnt to be false. He has learnt to wear many faces 'like dresses' (a home face, an office face, a street face, a host face), to say 'Goodbye' when he means 'good riddance', and to say 'glad to meet you' when he is not glad. He begs his son to teach him to 'unlearn' these false habits and to learn again how to laugh as he used to, because his laugh in the mirror shows only teeth, 'like a snake's bare fangs'.

Loss of innocence and cultural nostalgia: the 'once upon a time' stands for a time of genuine, warm African life. Hypocrisy: the false smiles and handshakes of modern society. Cultural conflict (Africa and the West): the poem mourns the loss of warm traditional values to cold modern manners. The innocence of children: the child, still genuine, is the teacher.

Tone: nostalgic, sad, regretful and bitter. Repetition: 'once upon a time', 'laugh', 'good-bye', which stress the loss. Simile: the laugh that is 'like a snake's bare fangs' shows that the new laughter is dangerous and false. Metaphor: wearing many faces 'like dresses' (a simile in form, but the idea of 'faces' as masks is a metaphor) shows personalities that can be put on and taken off. Irony: the father, an adult who should teach, begs to be taught by his son. The poem is written in free verse, close to speech, which suits its sincere feeling.

activity: What is the difference between 'laughing with the heart' and 'laughing with the teeth'? What does the speaker want his son to teach him?

title: African Poetry: 'Not My Business' by Niyi Osundare
summary: The poet, the poem's three episodes and final stanza, its themes of apathy and oppression, the refrain and its simple style.

p: Niyi Osundare is a Nigerian poet, born in Ikere-Ekiti. His poetry is known for strong social and political concerns, a love of common people and simple, musical language.

The poem is a political poem about apathy (not caring) and its price. It is set in a country ruled by force, and critics link it to the military rule of the 1990s in Nigeria. The speaker sees an unnamed, powerful 'they' take his neighbours away one by one. Akanni is picked up at night and bundled off. Then Danladi is taken. Then Chinwe suffers too. After each event the speaker does nothing and comforts himself with the refrain 'Not my business'. In the last stanza, 'they' come for the speaker, and now there is no one left to speak for him.

Political oppression: the poem criticises brutal rule. Apathy and complicity: the central theme. It attacks the 'every man for himself' attitude. The price of silence: silence in the face of injustice is not safe. It only delays one's own turn.

Tone: casual, detached and even sarcastic in the early stanzas, then panicked and fearful in the last. Refrain: 'Not my business' is repeated to show the speaker's deliberate, foolish carelessness. Names: Akanni (Yoruba), Danladi (Hausa) and Chinwe (Igbo) are from three of Nigeria's major groups, so the suffering cuts across all ethnic lines. Simple diction: the plain, story-like language reads like a news report, which makes the events seem chillingly normal. Structure: short stanzas with a repeating pattern, and a final stanza that breaks the pattern.

The lesson plan gives specific 'crimes' for the three victims (being 'too bold', stretching a mat 'too wide' and having 'ideas'). Those reasons are not part of the poem's message: what matters is that each is taken away by 'they' and the speaker does nothing. When you answer questions, speak of what the poem makes clear: arbitrary seizure by the powerful, the repeated refrain and the speaker's own turn at the end. Check the text of the poem in your anthology for the exact wording.

title: African Poetry: 'Night' by Wole Soyinka
summary: The poet, the meaning of Soyinka's 'Night' as a poem of fear and mortality, its imagery, tone, structure and devices.

p: Wole Soyinka (born 1934) is a Nigerian playwright, poet and essayist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986, the first African to do so. He is known for rich, dense language and for his strong views on freedom and injustice.

Night is normally a time of rest, but in this poem the speaker fears it. He wonders what kind of rest he can expect. The poem is spoken by a poet-figure who feels that he is as vulnerable as anyone who has been harmed in the dark. Night here is more than the time of day. It stands for human mortality, danger, the unknown and the end of life. In Yoruba tradition night is a dangerous time when wicked deeds are done, and life can be divided into morning, afternoon and night (old age). Critics link the poem to the violence, the war and the imprisonment of Soyinka's own time in Nigeria and to the loss of friends.

The poem uses images of fading and fear: a clam retreating into its shell, the light of the sea going out, a dimming crescent (moon), shadows falling through leaves and silent 'night thieves'. Night is personified, spoken of as a presence with power. The combination of images builds a mood of fear, loss and resignation.

Tone: anxious, mournful and resigned, with a trace of thoughtful acceptance. Structure: five stanzas, each building on the last, with enjambment (a thought running on across a stanza break) between stanzas two and three and three and four. The last stanza turns towards a faint hope but still ends with regret. Devices: personification of night, simile and metaphor, paradox, oxymoron (such as 'night children') and unusual word use that gives ordinary words deeper meaning.

The lesson plan describes images such as 'gourds of darkness' and 'metal leaves', and a speaker who is a worshipper at an altar. These do not match published readings of the poem. Use the imagery above, and always check the lines of the poem in your anthology.

activity: In 'Night', is night shown as a good thing, a bad thing or something else? Explain, using two images.

title: African Poetry: 'The Breasts of the Sea' by Syl Cheney-Coker
summary: The poet, the sea as a mothering and murdering force, the poem's allusions to wars, slavery and science, its tone and its devices.

p: Syl Cheney-Coker, born in Freetown in 1945, is a Sierra Leonean poet and novelist. His poems often deal with the history and politics of Africa and with exile. The poem is also known as 'The Breast of the Sea' and appears in his collection Stone Child and Other Poems.

The poem looks at the 20th century as a century of wars, slavery and colonialism, political failure and damage to the environment, and at what these did to Africa and to Europe. Its central symbol is the sea. The sea is a mother, whose 'breasts' feed and comfort. But it is also a place that holds the dead and the dumped waste of many conflicts and of unrestrained science. It keeps a record of history. The poem opens with a sense of loss, at the middle of the action, and moves through references to Noah's flood, the Middle Passage (the slave route), Darwin's theory of evolution and the sinking of the Titanic. Later stanzas turn to Sierra Leone, to the civil conflicts of Africa and to exile.

The shared violence between Africa and Europe (wars, slavery, empire); political failure and civil conflict (Sierra Leone and Nigeria); the sea as a source of both life and death; the link between knowledge and power and the harm of unrestrained science; and the survivors who are left with lasting wounds.

Images: the sea as a mother with 'breasts'; 'new islands' (conflicts that keep appearing); pollution and toxins; a broken (fractured) claw; blight (a plant disease) for the century's sickness; and images of bodily injury, such as a broken back or torn clothing, with a 'balm' that promises healing but may not heal.

Tone: reflective and serious. Mood: pessimistic, doubting that history's damage can be repaired. Devices: metaphor and personification of the sea; allusion to Noah, the Middle Passage, the Titanic and Darwin; and a shift in the meaning of the word 'children', from nations that were harmed to the poor who survive.

The lesson plan reads the poem as a personal 'homecoming' with the speaker's 'blood' mixing with the 'salt' of the sea. Published analyses focus instead on the sea as a witness and dumping ground of 20th-century violence and on the century's wounds. Use the reading above and check your anthology's text.

title: Non-African Poetry: 'Still I Rise' by Maya Angelou
summary: The poet, the speaker and her oppressors, the poem's themes of resilience and self-worth, its tone and its devices.

p: Maya Angelou (1928 to 2014) was an American poet, memoirist and civil rights activist. 'Still I Rise' is one of her best-known poems and has become an anthem of pride and resistance.

The speaker talks straight to those who try to put her down (racists, sexists and all who try to break her). She asks whether her confidence ('sassiness') and pride upset them. She says that however they 'write her down in history' with bitter, twisted lies, tread her in the dirt or try to kill her with hatefulness, she will always rise. She compares her certainty to the moon, the sun and the tides, and she compares her value to wealth ('oil wells', 'gold mines'). She calls herself 'a black ocean, leaping and wide' and, at the end, 'the dream and the hope of the slave'.

Resilience and defiance: the main theme, the refusal to be beaten. Overcoming oppression: the poem is about overcoming racial (Black) and gender (female) oppression. Self-worth and pride: a bold statement of pride and joy.

Tone: defiant, proud, triumphant, cheeky, angry at times and finally joyful. Refrain: 'Still I rise' ties the poem together like an anthem. Simile: 'like dust, I'll rise'; shoulders 'like teardrops'. Rhetorical questions: 'Does my sassiness upset you?' and 'Did you want to see me broken?' challenge the oppressor directly. Metaphor: she is a 'black ocean' and has 'gold mines' and 'oil wells' (symbols of great natural wealth). The poem uses short stanzas with a strong beat and plain, direct speech.

title: Non-African Poetry: 'She Walks in Beauty' by Lord Byron
summary: The poet, the poem's praise of a woman whose outer beauty comes from inner goodness, its themes, tone, rhyme scheme and devices.

p: George Gordon, Lord Byron (1788 to 1824) was an English poet of the Romantic movement, which valued feeling, nature and the individual. He wrote 'She Walks in Beauty' in 1814, after seeing a beautiful woman in black mourning dress at a party.

The speaker is amazed by a woman's beauty. He compares it to a clear, starry night. Her beauty is a perfect balance ('dark and bright') of light and shade, seen in her face and hair. The poem's main idea is that her outer beauty comes from her inner goodness. Her thoughts are 'serenely sweet', and her mind is at peace with the world, and her heart is innocent.

Beauty, outer and inner: true beauty is a harmony of the physical and the spiritual. Harmony and perfection: the poem delights in balance, in light and dark, and in calm. Innocence: the woman's innocent heart is the source of her beauty.

Tone: admiring, thoughtful, romantic and peaceful. Simile: the first line compares her to the night. Alliteration: 'cloudless climes and starry skies'. Personification: the woman's thoughts 'express' themselves on her face. Contrast: dark and bright, shade and light. Structure: three stanzas of six lines each, with a strict ABABAB rhyme scheme and iambic tetrameter (four iambs, or eight syllables, in a line: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM). This regular, musical rhythm matches the 'harmony' that the poem describes.

activity: Compare the tone of 'Still I Rise' with the tone of 'She Walks in Beauty'. How does the purpose of each poem (one to defy, one to admire) shape its tone? (300 words.)
